en: Preface to the *Ke xiū chán yào jué* (Engraved Essentials of the Practice of Dhyāna).
In the past, An Shigao and Dharmarakṣa translated various dhyāna sūtras; Sengguang, Tanyou, and others all cultivated their minds in accordance with these teachings.
Later, when Master Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong, Sengrui requested that he translate the essential methods of dhyāna practice. Thus, there have been many such individuals throughout history.
Since Bodhidharma came from the West and Master Sengchou arose in the East, this tradition has flourished greatly.

Reaching the middle period of the Tang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka masters Śubhakarasiṃha, Vajrabodhi, and Amoghavajra transmitted the Secret Dhyāna, which developed into a distinct school. What is transmitted here now combines both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings;

its principles distinguish between the Chinese and Sanskrit traditions and constitute a truly essential manual. Having first obtained several editions, I have collated them against the Tripitaka canon. Zhu Yingju [resides here].

A scholar is one who possesses integrity. You have planned to carve this [text] for its broad dissemination. I said: "Mitiān (Maitreya) once said: 'In meditative contemplation, one guards the profound;
by refining the subtle, one enters quiescence. As for what path to take, it is as clear as seeing something in the palm of one's hand.

To abandon this essential point and yet hope to realize the vision—would that not be difficult? Now, regarding the essential gateway to entering the Buddha-way, there is indeed nothing that surpasses this. Now, you—
To raise this up— who would not rejoice? Thus, in the winter of the fourth year of Tenmei,
the year of Jiachen (1784), the śramaṇa Zhìhuī of Bōmō compiled and edited these *Essential Instructions for Cultivating Dhyāna*.
The Northern Indian Brahmin Dhyāna Master Buddhapālita (translated into Chinese as Jue’ai) gave this brief explanation in response to inquiries.
Recorded verbatim by the śramaṇa Mingxun of the Chanlin Monastery in the Western Capital, with the assistance of the Vinaya Master Huizhi, a monk from India of the same monastery.
This was during the second year of the Yifeng era of the Great Tang, the Dingchou year.
Question: In this land, practitioners of Chan throughout both ancient and modern times have largely been unable to avoid the various obstacles and difficulties encountered in Chan practice.
Judging by this, it seems that the Chan masters here may not have fully realized the Dharma. Having lingered for so long, I have had no place to voice my doubts.

Now, unexpectedly, I have encountered the parable of the *tánhuā* (rare flower) shown by you; having received this instruction, I wish to return to my country immediately, for there will likely be no further opportunity to meet again. I humbly hope for your compassionate favor.

[The questioner] requested a full exposition of the essentials of dhyāna, hoping that practitioners would have a reliable point of reliance. [The Master] replied: "The methods of dhyāna are bestowed gradually;
it is not appropriate to explain them all at once. How could they be fully set forth?"
Question: I have heard that you intend to return to the West; once you gradually transmit [the teachings], they shall no longer have a place of reliance here.

Since the Buddha-dharma contains both permissions and prohibitions, I would be grateful if you would not obstruct this karmic opportunity. Answer: According to this, it is indeed worthy of compassion. However, I shall simply speak in accordance with whatever questions may arise.
Question: Some say that when the sutras speak of the firmness of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they refer to the third five-hundred-year period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.

Since that time is now far distant, it is not appropriate to practice meditation. According to this statement, is it appropriate to practice meditation? Answer: The sutras also state extensively that one should practice meditation.

If we rely on the fact that the Buddha is fundamentally never-extinguished (*aparinirvṛta*), what relevance do long or short periods of time have? Even in the present day in the West [India], [meditation is practiced].
Those who have attained the four dhyānas and eight samādhis are exceedingly numerous, beyond all calculation. If you say this is inconsistent [with your position], how so?

Among the three types of wisdom, dhyāna is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). How could it be appropriate at this time to permit only the study of hearing and reflection (*śruta* and *cintā*) while forbidding cultivation?
This statement relies exclusively on an extreme view and is not a comprehensive teaching. Although it cites Buddhist sūtras, there is nothing therein that is not erroneous.
Correct. Furthermore, to selectively cite a single passage from the sacred teachings to obscure its manifold meanings is surely the teaching of Māra.
One must examine this deeply; one must examine this deeply.

Question: Recently, I have observed that many practitioners of Chan lose their minds. Once this occurs, they find no further use for it and consequently abandon the myriad practices, spending their lives in vain.
For these reasons, I wish to cultivate other practices instead; may I not practice Chan? Answer: No.
Chan is the fifth of the six perfections (pāramitās) and is also the training in concentration (samādhi-śikṣā) among the three trainings. How could one do otherwise?
As for cultivation: suppose there is a person who dies from choking on food; does this mean one should simply not eat? That loss of mind is merely due to an unskillful method.
If one understands the skillful means, there will be no failure even among thousands or tens of thousands of attempts. Do not harbor doubt or fear; you must certainly practice it.
There was once a monk in Northern India who constantly practiced extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) but did not study meditative concentration (*samādhi*). At that time, he was reciting the sutras.
Suddenly, a deity came and covered his mouth, saying: "Your hearing and reflection are sufficient; why do you not practice meditation to verify them?
Even if you cultivate other practices, if you do not study meditative concentration, you have not fully attained the Buddha-dharma."

Question: For one whose nature is prone to great distraction, by what means can they attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through practice? Answer: Even a monkey is capable of sitting in meditation; how much more so should a human being not be able to do so?
The difficulty in practicing concentration is simply due to the fact that one has never practiced it in previous lives.
If you do not practice now, how will you ever attain it in the future? How could it be that after such a long duration, one still fails to attain it? One must look forward with renewed hope.
When? The Sūtra says: "Hearing and reflection are like being outside the gate; meditative practice is like beginning to enter.

Even the merit of cultivating meditation for as little as a single thought-moment is immeasurable. How could one not study this throughout an entire lifetime? For those who have not yet been able to master it entirely, it is fortunate that they may cultivate both together.
Although those who lecture may discuss the methods of meditation extensively, they are merely like those who describe food without ever having tasted it.

As for the practice of dhyāna, it is like beginning a meal of fine delicacies. In the past, there was a king who, having heard of the benefits of dhyāna, attended to the affairs of state while simultaneously practicing meditation.
How much more so should those who have left the household life—having shaved their hair, eliminated worldly distractions, and stilled the mind to be free from concerns—not study this?
How could they not be considered human beings [if they do not]?

Question: Is the practice of Chan limited solely to sitting? Answer: What a way of speaking! For one with a conditioned body, it is essential to train interchangeably while easily transitioning through the four modes of deportment;
how could it be limited to sitting alone? To sit exclusively invites many demonic obstacles.
Question: Regarding the four modes of deportment, what is the method for sitting? Answer: One sits cross-legged and upright. As for the method of crossing the legs:

one may place the left foot over the right, or the right foot over the left; both are permissible. If crossing the legs is not convenient, one may sit half-cross-legged. The method for the half-crossed position is specifically to place the right foot over the left.
Both hands are to be extended with palms facing upward, with the right hand placed over the left; the left must never be placed over the right.
This is for pressing the right side. One must close the eyes and the mouth, with the tongue placed against the upper palate or perhaps against the teeth.
These actions, such as closing the eyes and mouth, should not be done too tightly; indeed, in all matters, relaxation is valued over constraint. Do not be restrictive or forceful.

For those not yet accustomed to keeping the eyes closed, one may open them slightly as needed. If one becomes somewhat fatigued from sitting for a long time, one should immediately adjust one’s posture so as not to give rise to suffering;
all other matters should be handled accordingly.
Question: In this land, it has been traditionally transmitted that because the right hand and so forth move more frequently, one who sits must press the left over the right.

Now, this is exactly the opposite of that [Western] practice; I do not understand why this is so. Answer: Among the Buddhas of the Western regions, from the time of the Buddha until the present, the methods of sitting have been handed down in this very manner.
These are all mudrā practices. That this land has unilaterally altered them is something I have not yet fully investigated.

Question: When practicing seated meditation, if one leans against an object or the body happens to slouch or lean forward and backward, is it permissible to remain sitting according to one's natural inclination? Answer:
One must necessarily sit upright with the body straightened. If the body is leaning or crooked, illness and pain will inevitably arise.
Question: I have respectfully heard about sitting; what is the practice of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*)? Answer: Walking meditation refers to *caṅkrama*.
One should follow a level ground, ranging from twenty steps to forty-five steps or more, and perform the walking meditation therein.
When walking, cover the left hand; bend the thumb into the palm and clench the remaining four fingers around the thumb to form a fist.
Cover the right hand and grasp the left wrist. Then sit upright for a short while, collecting the mind and causing it to abide—meaning to fix it on the tip of the nose and so forth—and then proceed.
When walking, do not be too hurried nor too slow; simply maintain the continuity of the mind.

Upon reaching the boundary, immediately turn the body each day and return toward the place from which one came. Stand still for a short while, and as before, walk again. When walking, keep the eyes open.

When one stops, one immediately closes [the gate]. After practicing in this manner for a long time, one gradually becomes weary and ceases the walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). This is done only during the day; one does not walk at night. Question:
May many people practice walking meditation together in the same place? Answer: They must remain somewhat apart from one another; they may not be too close.

Question: If this is indeed the case regarding their practice, why did the sages of old not speak of it at all? I beg you to point to specific instances and explain them in detail, so that I may follow their example and establish a new precedent.
Answer: In the kingdom of Uḍḍiyāna, there are places where the Buddha practiced walking meditation as well as places where Maitreya Bodhisattva practiced walking meditation;
in both cases, stone boundaries have been carved to mark the areas. These remain clearly visible even today, and all who see them pay homage from afar, none daring to tread upon them.
As for the place where the Bodhisattva practiced his path, if people enter therein, they desire to measure its length;
yet whether it be extended or shortened, no one is ultimately able to determine the number of steps. Such traces have frequently appeared in various lands regarding this matter of walking meditation.

This is indeed commonplace; it has been evident throughout antiquity and the present. There should be no cause for confusion. Alas! Even regarding such a minor matter, people here remain deluded. Question:

What is the difference between circumambulating a stūpa and *caṅkrama* (walking meditation)? Answer: One who practices *caṅkrama* walks straight back and forth; how could this be the same as circumambulation?
Furthermore, a stūpa is a place where many people come and go; one must not practice *caṅkrama* therein.
Question: In this region, there are those who walk against the sun and call it "right-turning" (pradakṣiṇa). I do not know if this is correct. Answer:

In the Western Regions, when circumambulating a stūpa, one always follows the direction of the sun; there has never been a practice of walking against it. (This point arises as a secondary digression and is not the primary subject of this treatise.)
Question: I have respectfully heard about walking; what is the method for standing? Answer: Standing consists of straightening the body, collecting the mind, and standing upright.

The two hands are held in the same manner as when walking. If one stands thus for a long time and begins to feel weary, or if the two feet seem to leave the ground, or if such sensations arise, one should then rest and instead practice standing, sitting, or other postures.

Question: I have respectfully heard the rules for staying [awake]. What is the method for lying down? Answer: One lies on the right side with the body touching the ground, using the palm of the right hand as a pillow.
The left hand is extended and placed upon the left thigh. Both feet are extended and stacked one upon the other, joined together, and one lies down.
Those who are ill may lie down as they find comfortable.

Question: Are all the rules of conduct within the various modes of deportment (iryāpatha) considered mudrās? Answer: As practiced above in meditation—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
whether bending or extending, advancing or retreating; and whether with the hands, feet, left or right sides—one by one, all of these are mudrās.
Question: To what vehicle (yāna) does the aforementioned method of practicing dhyāna through the [four] modes of deportment (īryāpatha) belong? Answer: It belongs to the Mahāyāna. Question:
Is it not the case that the method of practicing dhyāna using the four modes of deportment is also present among the followers of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists (tīrthika)?

Answer: This method of dhyāna did not exist even at the outset for the Hīnayāna; how could it possibly exist among non-Buddhists? For those of heterodox schools fundamentally intend to undergo suffering, such as standing on one foot or remaining inverted.
Hanging [the mind] upon the True Dharma serves to dispel weariness and fatigue, while its majestic deportment is easy to maintain. In the Hinayana, there may be some degree of progress;

in the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), there is none at all. Question: Both non-Buddhists and those of the three vehicles possess meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi). They both quiet the mind and dispel external objects. I do not yet understand what distinguishes them. Answer:
The non-Buddhists cling to a self while practicing meditation; those of the Lesser Vehicle calculate dharmas while cultivating concentration.
In the Mahāyāna practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā, both person and phenomena are eliminated—this is the distinction between them.
Question: One who wishes to study dhyāna—what should be taken as the preliminary expedient? Answer: First, one must give rise to great compassion and forever abandon thoughts of seeking revenge;
only then can one practice dhyāna. Should greed or anger arise, they must be swiftly eliminated through repentance, like striking water with a staff.
It opens for a moment and then closes again; as evil thoughts continue in succession, one cannot learn Chan. Question:
When first beginning to learn Chan, is it possible to immediately contemplate the signless? Answer: One must enter by means of skillful means through gradual stages.
"I have not yet seen one who can suddenly manifest the signless (*animitta*).
Question: "How does one proceed gradually? Answer: "For such an intermediate practitioner, one causes the mind to first dwell within the single city of Chang'an, ensuring it does not go outside.
In this manner, one dwells gradually within a single monastery, a single room, and even at the tip of the nose. If the mind..."
If it does not remain, bring it back and cause it to abide.
Question: What is the method for the tip of the nose? Answer: One should imagine a single drop of dew hanging from the tip of the nose and dwell the mind upon observing this.
Question: Once this visualization has been accomplished, what should one observe next? Answer: Next, visualize within the navel a fine spring-like stream as if within sand.
If this visualization is accomplished, one may see radiance or various things within the abdomen. Next, observe the crown of the head, which is shaped like the mouth of a jar.
It penetrates straight down through the body, reaching into the earth below. Once this visualization has been established, one next visualizes the crown of the head;
having visualized the crown, one then visualizes four finger-widths above it, causing the mind to abide there.

From this point onward, the body gradually becomes autonomous, and one subsequently attains entry into the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*). Proceeding from the shallow to the deep, the process is like the gradual ascent of a ladder.
Question: Is it also possible to transcend from the perception of the tip of the nose and immediately attain the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*)?
Answer: It is like a person who, while originally seeking copper or iron in the sand and soil, might instead find gold. This case is just like that.

By taking the tip of the nose as a condition, one may enter the perception of the crown of the head, or enter the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), or attain signlessness and so forth. Such is the process of transcending the sequence in the interim.
This is indeterminate. Question:
A sutra says, "If the mind has a dwelling place, it is not truly dwelling. Or it says, "The mind relying on objects is movement, not dhyāna.
If one takes the tip of the nose as an object, is this not a case of having a dwelling place? Answer: Once the perception of the nose and so forth is established, one immediately abandons it.
Furthermore, when one observes other signs and discards them as soon as they are attained, how can this constitute "abiding"? Question:

When focusing on the tip of the nose and so forth, it is through the accumulation of mental attention that [the sign] is accomplished. Once the mind has accumulated such attention for a long time, it will certainly be difficult to discard.

Why then would one suddenly discard the nose and subsequently attain focus on the navel? Answer: This was originally undertaken as a formal commitment (*samaya*). Although it was attained, one did not abide in it; once the visualization was completed, it naturally [ceased].
Disenchantment. Once disenchantment has arisen, it is very easy to relinquish [the objects of attachment].

Question: According to the holy teachings, those who first enter the Path are first instructed in the five *smṛtyupasthānas* (foundations of mindfulness) and so forth; why is it not so in this case? Answer:
The five *sthāpanā-cittas* (stabilizing the mind) and [methods such as] focusing on the tip of the nose are each distinct approaches. That which I have received and inherited relies solely upon this.
Question: There is a sacred teaching which states that if one does not first study extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not permitted.
May those with little learning cultivate dhyāna? Answer: As in the approach transmitted from my Upādhyāya and Ācārya, one may simply study dhyāna directly, without asking [such questions].

There is much learning and little learning. Among these, those who first possess much learning are the most preeminent. However, some who possess much learning may instead become inverted, becoming increasingly frivolous and distracted;
there are indeed those whose much learning accords with meditative concentration, as well as those whose it does not.

Question: The wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation arise in a sequential order. Since one who lacks the wisdom of hearing from extensive learning cannot possess it, how can the wisdom of cultivation arising from meditative concentration ever be produced?
Answer: Suppose there were a person who did not recognize a single character, yet understood the methods of meditation;

this too constitutes extensive learning. It does not necessarily require the wide searching of texts and phrases. Cūḍapanthaka could recite "broom" but forgot "winnowing fan," yet he became a great Arhat. How could this be... [omitted] ...?
"Is it through much learning? For now, let this serve as proof; it is not necessarily the case for all. Question:
"Are those who maintain the precepts and those who violate them both able to study dhyāna? Answer: "Regardless of whether one maintains or violates the precepts, both are able to study dhyāna.
However, first purifying and maintaining the precepts is especially the foremost [requirement]."
Question: The holy teachings state that when śīla is pure, samādhi manifests before one. How can a person who has broken the precepts cultivate meditative concentration? Answer:

What constitutes upholding the precepts for a śrāvaka is precisely what constitutes breaking the precepts for a bodhisattva. In the Hīnayāna, once a grave offense is committed, one is permanently discarded; how then could they cultivate dhyāna?
The statement that "if śīla is impure, samādhi does not manifest" is based on this [Hīnayāna] teaching. However, within the Mahāyāna...
Simply being able to still the mind is true repentance. Because true repentance causes transgressions to cease and precepts to arise, one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

This indicates that there is a preliminary entry into the Vaipulya repentance, through which one attains the signs of the extinction of offenses; only after further cultivating the categories of precepts does one begin to practice meditation.

Question: By means of what dharma should one practice so that the mind quickly attains concentration? Answer: One who seeks concentration too hastily is, in fact, being indolent. Be careful not to seek speed.
Rather, simply be able to leave behind discursive thoughts and cease all攀缘 (pān-yuan, objective attachments). Whether concentration is attained or not, neither seek it nor do not seek it.
"Simply do not harbor thoughts or calculations; this is great diligence. In the kingdom of Udyāna there was a monk who sat for a long time but could not attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
He consequently abandoned his practice. Suddenly, a deity manifested as a human being and appeared before him, grinding an iron hammer.
The monk asked, "What is this for? The deity replied, "I wish to make a needle from it. The monk said, "How can it ever be completed? The deity said, "If you do not cease, it will be finished."

The monk subsequently attained realization and returned to practicing dhyāna, thereby attaining the fruits of the Path. Later, he again entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Because he remained in this state of cessation, he is still present even now. He simply made diligent effort toward the elimination of discursive thought; having attained such concentration, why worry that it would not be swift?

Question: What are the signs within meditative concentration (*samādhi*)? Answer: The signs of concentration are extremely numerous; I shall cite three or five for now. Sometimes the head takes on the appearance of a man;

sometimes one perceives that the body is covered in many impurities and greasiness. These are signs of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), and one should immediately alter one’s deportment (*īryāpatha*), or temporarily cease [the practice].
Or, one may perceive as if insects or ants are crawling upon the body; or again, like...
If clouds, white cotton cloths, or similar things arise from one's back, do not be alarmed and do not touch them with your hands.
Or, it may be like drops of oil flowing down from the head and face, or one may see light at the place where one sits. These are all signs preceding meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If, while sitting or standing for a long time, the body becomes weary and fatigued, and one hears the sound of finger-snapping or the sound of touching a door nearby, one should immediately depart.
Whether in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or during sleep and rest, these are the auspicious deities who, being well aware of human fatigue, come to provide an alerting warning.
Alternatively, if one feels the body becoming light and buoyant and experiences pleasure, this is a precursor sign of the supernormal power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*).

If it is light and buoyant but accompanied by suffering, this is an increase of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). If certain parts of the body feel hot, this is a sign of the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*). Or, if one sees...

The illumination of a single room is a preliminary sign of the first dhyāna. Or, if one perceives wondrous and marvelous fragrances unequaled in the world, this is a sign that meditative concentration has been achieved.
Such instances as these cannot be described in full; however, whenever one perceives such signs—whether favorable or adverse—one must not grasp at them to give rise to sorrow or joy.
One should simply take the original object as the focal point and settle the mind in tranquility.

Question: Since a practitioner of seated meditation should not forcibly suppress the body and mind, if one perceives such things as the crawling of insects and ants and suppresses these feelings so they do not arise, does this not constitute a forced suppression?
Answer: One should not employ force when meditative concentration has not yet been attained; once one gradually enters concentration, there is no fault in employing force.
Question: When emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), what are the appropriate times and conditions? Answer: A beginner in concentration should first establish a commitment, such as:
"I shall emerge from absorption after a certain period of time, or when the bell rings, or at a specific hour or watch. Having made such a commitment, one should then emerge.

Thereafter, one enters dhyāna; this must necessarily be so. As for those who enter meditative absorption and remain for as long as several kalpas or for periods of seven days, two days, or one day, these durations—whether long or short—are entirely in accordance with the state of their minds. When wishing to emerge from concentration, one first moves from the mind.
Once the mind has moved, the vital energies and channels gradually become unobstructed; thereafter, one slowly moves the body and rises. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"The World-Honored One arose from meditative concentration with composure."
Question: If demonic obstacles arise, how should they be dispelled? Answer: Simply practice by understanding how to easily shift and release oneself within the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*);

then there will be no demonic obstacles. Be careful not to force yourself and thereby create suffering for yourself; the Path arises from ease, unlike the various ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
If you understand this message, demonic obstacles will naturally disappear. If they still do not disappear, then it is appropriate to simply let them go.
Alternatively, one may recite and study the sūtras and śāstras, even to the point of entering marketplaces to let the eyes wander and the mind relax; this will surely dispel the work of Māra.

However, if there is only a "dhyāna-illness," it should be treated according to the methods of dhyāna as prescribed by the scriptural teachings; it is not something that can be cured merely by acupuncture, medicine, or other such means.

Question: Is there a method for preventing demonic interference while practicing seated meditation? Answer: Whenever one wishes to study meditation, one should first give rise to compassionate vows, thinking:
"As I now cultivate meditative concentration, I shall certainly attain Bodhi and extensively benefit all sentient beings.

I pray only that the Triple Gem, the various celestial deities, and others will protect my person, ensuring that no calamities or obstacles arise. Having made this vow each time, one should then practice meditation. Furthermore, within the meditation hall...
On the upper portions of the four walls, paint many images of holy monks (*ārya-bhikṣu*), all depicted in the posture of full-lotus meditation (*paryaṅka-bandha*) and deep concentration (*samādhi*).

These images of the holy monks should be made somewhat large; they should further be honored with offerings of flowers and incense. Below them, paint images of various ordinary monks (*prākṛta-bhikṣu*).

It is slightly better to make them small; they should be the size of a human being and depicted in the posture of meditating. Then, one may practice meditation within them to prevent the occurrence of demonic obstacles.
Question: Is it permissible to practice seated meditation inside a Buddha hall? Answer: Seated meditation should be practiced in a quiet room, beneath a tree, or among burial mounds.
Regarding sitting in the open air and so forth, it need not be done inside a Buddha hall.

Question: Is it permissible for many people to sit together in one place for meditation? Answer: It is indeed permissible; however, they should sit with their faces turned away from one another and their backs toward each other.
They must not face one another. If there are many people, a single lamp or candle may be lit at night; if there are few, it is unnecessary.
Question: Must one wear and maintain the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe) while practicing seated meditation? Answer: It is permissible to remain naked; there is no fixed requirement. Question:
Does a practitioner of meditation always maintain mindfulness at all times? Answer: With the exception of the time for defecating and urinating, one must always maintain mental focus at other times.

Question: Concentrated mind is called *śamatha* (calm abiding). Does *vipaśyanā* (insight) exist within *śamatha*? Answer: Simply do not study it [separately]; you shall know it for yourself when the time comes. Question:
Can a practitioner of seated meditation also engage in upholding the sutras, preaching, and so forth? Answer: One may engage in all such things as long as one has the strength to sustain them.

Although this is so, among all types of karma, the karma of dhyāna is the most supreme. For this reason, in the West (India), the superior rooms and superior offerings were first granted to the *dhyāna-masters*, while those who taught the Sūtras and Vinaya were assigned to the middle and lower quarters.
Question: Can those who practice dhyāna (meditation) avoid the evil realms at the time of death? Answer: It is like being in an extremely remote and perilous place;

if one encounters bandits without carrying a bow and arrows, one will surely be in danger. The body is likewise. Having already dwelt in impermanence, if one does not cultivate dhyāna beforehand, the mind will inevitably become distracted at the moment of death, leading to rebirth mostly in the evil realms.
One whose mind is concentrated and self-possessed will be free from delusion at the time of death. There is no...
Because they have overturned their delusions and are born into a realm of goodness according to their minds, they aspire to realize the fruit within this very life;

how much more so, then, will they avoid the evil realms at the time of death? There are also those who study meditation throughout a lifetime without attaining realization, yet attain it just as they are about to relinquish their lives.
After such a person dies, their complexion does not change and their body remains supple; these are the signs of such a one.
The Zen Master has repeatedly said: "Those who learn through hearing and reflection are merely practicing with a good prescription;

it is only upon reaching the wisdom of cultivation that one is truly taking the wondrous medicine. Though one may possess extensive learning and practices such as giving and morality, if one does not yet practice serenity meditation (*dhyāna*), they cannot yet be called a person who cultivates the Path.
He further stated: "Zen concentration (*samādhi*) is the smelting away of coarseness and vulgarity, and the refining of the spiritual intelligence."

Those of you who possess a taste for these matters should especially maintain this practice. However, as we have only briefly encountered a master of the profound mysteries, I have inquired only as previously described.

Due to the constraints of this short time, I have not been able to provide a comprehensive and detailed account; you should therefore consult the Golden Tablets in further detail and apply them accordingly.
One fascicle of the Essential Secret Instructions for Cultivating Dhyāna.
Completed copying at Kōmyō on the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the third year of the Jōhō era.
